bib.title: Inference After Model Selection (Chapter 20, Computer Age Statistical Inference: Algorithms, Evidence, and Data Science)

question: How can we assess the accuracy of an estimate or interval when the model or target was chosen from the same data?
hypothesis: Data-based selection inflates apparent accuracy and bias unless the inference accounts for it, via simultaneous/FCR intervals, bootstrap-with-bagging, empirical Bayes shrinkage, or frequentist checks on Bayes estimates.
contributions: Five vignettes: simultaneous intervals (Scheffe, Tukey, BYq FCR), bootstrap accuracy after Cp selection with bagging and infinitesimal-jackknife SE, selection bias via Tweedie's formula, Bayes-frequentist delta-method SE

results.claim: Ignoring Cp model selection, bootstrap standard errors of the fitted curve at c=-2 are 3.97 (fixed cubic) instead of 5.98 (adaptive Cp/OLS): selection adds more than 50%.
results.note: c=-2 read from the rendered figure caption; the text layer dropped the minus sign (sign confirmed by image).

results.claim: Averaged over c in [-2.2, 2], adaptive standard errors are 43% larger than fixed-degree ones, so naive 95% intervals would be roughly 43% too short.
Bagging reduces the Cp/OLS standard errors by about 12%; IJ bagged SE over bootstrap SE averages 0.88.
results.setup: IJ-based SE of bagged estimate / bootstrap SE of t(c,x)
results.note: Fig 20.5 caption gives adaptive/smoothed = 1.14, consistent with 1/0.88.

results.claim: Cp selected linear (m=1) in 19% of 4000 bootstrap samples, and those cases shift the estimate at c=-2 about 10 units down (jumpiness).
Infinitesimal-jackknife external SD of the m=1 selection proportion is 0.24, versus binomial internal SE 0.006.
Scheffe 95% simultaneous intervals are wider than separate t intervals by a factor 2.19 (k=4.30 vs t=1.97).
results.setup: diabetes data n=442, p=10, q=432, sigma-hat=54.2
results.quote: wider than the t intervals (20.7) by a factor of 2.19

results.claim: Scheffe constant k_{p,q}^{(0.95)} equals 4.30 for p=10, q=432.
results.quote: equals 4.30 for p D 10, q D

results.claim: BYq FCR control at q=0.05: 565 declared non-null, 17 non-covering, FCR 17/565=0.030; 14 were null (FDP 0.025).
results.setup: simulation N=10,000, 9000 nulls, 1000 non-null mu~N(-3,1), q=0.05; declared cases z<=-2.77

results.claim: BYq intervals are accurate but not correct: the Bayes 95% interval (z-3)/2 +- 1.96/sqrt2 has half the width and slope 1/2 versus 1.
results.quote: They are half as wide as the BYq limits, and have slope 1=2 rather than 1.

results.claim: Tweedie estimate for prostate gene 610 shrinks z=5.29 to 4.03.
results.setup: prostate data N=6033 genes, 4th-degree log-polynomial fit of f(z), sigma=1
results.quote: For gene 610, with z610 D 5:29, Tweedie’s estimate is 4.03.

results.claim: At z=3.5 Tweedie gives E{mu|z}=1.96 and fdr=0.15, so about 85% of genes near 3.5 are non-null with average effect about 2.31.
Under normal prior, Tweedie reduces to (almost) James-Stein; the curve would be a straight line through origin with slope 0.22.
Tweedie correction removes selection bias in simulation: uncorrected top-20 differences shifted about one unit right of zero, corrected centred at zero with no added variance.
results.setup: 100 datasets of N=1000, exponential-normal mixture, natural spline df=5, top 20 z per dataset (2000 differences)
results.quote: shifted one unit to the right of zero

results.claim: Frequentist delta-method SE for a Bayesian-lasso posterior mean: 0.186 vs Bayes posterior SE 0.203 for patient 322 (9% smaller; averages 5% smaller across 442 patients).
results.setup: diabetes n=442, p=10, sigma=1 rescaled, prior exp(-lambda|beta|_1) lambda=0.37, MCMC B=10,000
results.note: Fig 20.9 legend prints Bayes SE as .205 versus 0.203 in text (20.56).

results.claim: Posterior cdf at c=2.5 for theta_322 is 0.687 with frequentist SE 0.325; 90% credible interval (2.08, 2.73) has endpoint SEs about 0.185, 28% of its length.
Cp minimised at cubic: Cp values (minus 80,000) 71887,1132,1412,667,1591,1811,2758 for degrees 0-6.

results.claim: Tukey simultaneous pairwise intervals are narrower than Scheffe: half-widths 2.95..4.44 vs 3.74..5.58 in units sigma-hat/sqrt(n), p=2..6, n=20.

limits: Authors: no overarching theory for inference after model selection; the chapter is vignettes (p.394).
Authors cannot say how far the Cp/OLS bootstrap-smoothed estimates are from optimal (Notes, p.413).
Scheffe and BYq intervals are 'accurate but not correct' (Fisherian); no formal definition of correct (p.399, p.402).
Theorem 20.4 SEs for the posterior cdf are large and the delta-method cdf can leave [0,1]; improved intervals are in Efron (2015).
Simulations are single designs (N=10,000 BYq; 100x1000 Tweedie); no seeds given.
practices: Do not set usual +-1.96 intervals on the R cases chosen by an FDR rule; use false-coverage-rate control such as BYq with alpha_R=1-Rq/N (Sec 20.1, p.399-400).
When model selection (e.g. Cp) is part of the estimator, bootstrap the whole select-then-fit algorithm to get honest standard errors (Sec 20.2, p.403).
Bag (bootstrap-smooth) a discontinuous selection estimator and get its SE from the infinitesimal jackknife using stored counts N_bj without a second bootstrap (Sec 20.2, p.405-406).
Report external uncertainty of selection frequencies (sdIJ), not the binomial internal SE (p.407).
Correct winner's-curse extremes with empirical Bayes shrinkage, Tweedie's formula E{mu|z}=z+sigma^2 l'(z) (Sec 20.3, p.408).
Restrict the catalog of comparisons (e.g. pairwise differences, Tukey) to get narrower simultaneous intervals than Scheffe (p.399, Notes 2).
Check Bayes estimates frequentistically with the delta-method SE, especially under convenience priors (Sec 20.4, p.412-413).

terms.definition: a catalog of parameters of possible interest, with an interval for each such that all contain their parameters with fixed probability, typically 0.95
FCR(A)=E{r/R}, the expected proportion of non-coverages among R selected intervals
the tendency of unusually good (or bad) comparative performances not to repeat themselves
averaging bootstrap replications of an estimator, s(x)=(1/B) sum t(x*_b), to smooth a discontinuous rule
E{mu|z}=z+sigma^2 l'(z), l'(z)=d/dz log f(z), posterior mean in terms of the marginal density
intervals have the claimed overall frequentist coverage but may mislead for individual cases
